## What Do Vision Transformers Actually Learn? {#sec-vit-internals}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Sources for this section"}

| # | Source | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Do Vision Transformers See Like CNNs?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.08810) | CKA analysis, 5 key ViT-vs-CNN differences |
| 2 | [An Image is Worth 16x16 Words (ViT)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) | Attention distance by depth, positional embedding similarity |
| 3 | [DINO: Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised ViTs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294) | Self-attention maps contain semantic segmentation info |

:::

You have built your ViT-based visual search engine, and it is working well. It outperforms your old CNN, especially on queries that require understanding the *meaning* of a product rather than just its visual texture. But something nags at you. When a customer searches for "vintage leather messenger bag," the ViT retrieves excellent results: aged leather, brass buckles, the right proportions. Your CNN retrieved results that *looked* similar — brown bags with similar textures — but missed the semantic concept of "vintage." You want to understand *why*. What is the ViT doing differently inside? Are its internal representations just fancier versions of CNN features, or something fundamentally new?

This section answers that question by presenting five key findings from Raghu et al. (2021), who systematically compared the internal representations of ViTs and CNNs using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA). The results are striking and have important practical implications for how you choose, interpret, and deploy these models.

### How to Compare Representations: CKA {#sec-cka}

Before diving into the findings, we need a tool for comparing what two different neural networks (or two layers within the same network) have learned. This is harder than it sounds: layer representations live in high-dimensional spaces with different dimensions, and neurons can be permuted without changing the function. We need a comparison metric that is invariant to these superficial differences.

**Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)** provides exactly this. Given two representation matrices $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p_1}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p_2}$ (the activations of $m$ examples at two different layers), CKA measures their similarity via:

$$
\text{CKA}(\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{L}) = \frac{\text{HSIC}(\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{L})}{\sqrt{\text{HSIC}(\mathbf{K}, \mathbf{K}) \cdot \text{HSIC}(\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{L})}}
$$ {#eq-cka}

where $\mathbf{K} = \mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top$ and $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}^\top$ are Gram matrices, and HSIC (Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion) measures statistical dependence between the representations. CKA ranges from 0 (completely different) to 1 (identical up to rotation and scaling), and is invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling. In other words, it compares *what information* the layers encode, not *how* they encode it.

With CKA in hand, let us examine what makes ViT representations different.

### Finding 1: ViTs Have More Uniform Representations Across Layers {#sec-uniform-representations}

This first finding is subtle but consequential. If you compute CKA similarity between every pair of layers in a ViT and plot it as a heatmap, you see something strikingly different from a CNN. In a ResNet, the heatmap shows clear block-diagonal structure: early layers (which detect edges and textures) are similar to each other but very different from late layers (which detect objects and scenes). There are sharp transitions between the "stages" of the ResNet where the representation changes character.

In a ViT, the heatmap is far more uniform. Lower and higher layers show much greater similarity to each other than in a ResNet. There are no sharp stage transitions. Instead, the representation evolves gradually and continuously from input to output.

What does this mean practically? ViT representations at different depths are more interchangeable than CNN representations. A feature from ViT layer 4 and a feature from ViT layer 20 encode more overlapping information than the corresponding CNN layers would. This matters for feature extraction: if you are using intermediate features (say, for a detection head or a VLM connector), you have more flexibility in *which* ViT layer to tap into.

### Finding 2: ViTs Aggregate Global Information from Layer One {#sec-early-global}

Here is where it gets interesting. This is perhaps the most important finding. In a CNN, the receptive field grows incrementally: layer 1 sees a $3 \times 3$ neighborhood, layer 2 sees $5 \times 5$, and it takes dozens of layers before the receptive field covers the full image. Global information (like the relationship between a product's label and its packaging) is only available in the deepest layers.

In a ViT, self-attention allows every patch to attend to every other patch from layer one. And ViTs *use* this capability. Raghu et al. measured the **mean attention distance** for each head: the average spatial distance (in patch coordinates) between the query patch and the patches it attends to, weighted by attention weights:

$$
d_\text{attn}(h, \ell) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} A^{(h,\ell)}_{ij} \cdot \|p_i - p_j\|
$$ {#eq-attention-distance}

where $A^{(h,\ell)}_{ij}$ is the attention weight from patch $i$ to patch $j$ in head $h$ at layer $\ell$, and $p_i, p_j$ are the 2D spatial positions of the patches.

The results reveal a fascinating pattern: **in the lowest layers, attention heads show high variance in their attention distance.** Some heads attend locally (small distances, like convolutions), while other heads attend globally (large distances, spanning the entire image). As depth increases, attention distance increases for all heads until they are all global in the deepest layers.

![Mean attention distance across layers for each head in ViT-L/16. In lower layers, some heads attend locally while others attend globally. In deeper layers, all heads attend globally. Source: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), Appendix.](Vision Transformers and VLMs/images/vit-attention-distance-by-depth.png){#fig-attention-distance}

This is the first crucial difference from CNNs: ViTs have access to global context from the very first layer, and they learn to use it. The network develops a *division of labor*. Some early heads handle local texture information (similar to what convolution layers capture), while others handle global context (which CNNs cannot access until much deeper). This dual strategy may explain why ViTs are particularly strong at tasks requiring global understanding.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: ViTs just learn convolutions internally"}
Some researchers initially assumed that ViT attention heads simply re-learn convolution-like local filters, and that ViTs are just a roundabout way of doing what CNNs already do. This is wrong. While *some* early-layer heads do learn local attention patterns (attending to immediate neighbors, similar to small convolutional kernels), *other* heads in the very same layer attend globally across the entire image. This mix of local and global attention from layer 1 is something CNNs architecturally cannot do. Furthermore, the CKA analysis from Raghu et al. shows that the features learned by the global attention heads are *qualitatively different* from anything in a ResNet. The lower 60 layers of a ResNet are similar only to the *local* heads of early ViT layers. The global heads learn representations that have no CNN counterpart.
:::

Raghu et al. found a critical scale effect: when trained only on ImageNet (without large-scale pre-training), larger ViT models (ViT-L/16, ViT-H/14) *fail to learn local attention patterns* in early layers, and their performance suffers accordingly. Smaller models (ViT-B/32) still learn local attention even on ImageNet alone. This suggests that learning local processing (which CNNs get for free) is important, and that ViTs need sufficient data to discover it. It is a concrete manifestation of the inductive bias trade-off we discussed in @sec-inductive-bias.

### Finding 3: Skip Connections Carry Most of the Signal {#sec-skip-connections}

ViTs rely on residual connections even more heavily than CNNs. Raghu et al. measured the norm ratio $\|\mathbf{z}_\ell\| / \|f(\mathbf{z}_\ell)\|$ at each layer, where $\mathbf{z}_\ell$ is the skip connection representation and $f(\mathbf{z}_\ell)$ is the transformation from the attention or MLP sub-layer. In ViTs, this ratio is much higher than in ResNets. The skip connections dominate. Most information flows through the "highway" of residual connections, with each attention and MLP layer making relatively small incremental updates.

There is an interesting phase transition in how the CLS token and spatial tokens use skip connections differently. In the first half of the network, the CLS token is primarily propagated through skip connections (the attention/MLP layers contribute little to the CLS representation), while spatial patch tokens receive significant updates from the attention layers. In the second half, this reverses: the CLS token starts receiving large attention-mediated updates (aggregating spatial information for classification), while spatial tokens rely more on skip connections to preserve their local information.

This has a practical consequence. If you remove the skip connection at any single block in the middle of a ViT, accuracy drops by about 4%, and the layer representations on either side of the removed connection become *partitioned*, unable to communicate. Skip connections are not just a training convenience in ViTs; they are an essential information highway.

### Finding 4: Spatial Information Persists Until the Final Layer {#sec-spatial-persistence}

This finding surprised the research community: ViT spatial tokens preserve their local spatial information far better than CNN features at corresponding depths. If you measure how much each spatial token in the final Transformer layer "remembers" its original patch location (using CKA between the token and its input patch), ViT tokens at interior positions are highly localized — each token is most similar to its corresponding input region.

This is counterintuitive because self-attention is global. You might expect that after 24 layers of global attention, every token would become a global mixture with no spatial specificity. But the combination of local attention heads in early layers, strong skip connections, and the CLS token's role as a separate aggregator allows spatial tokens to maintain their local character.

The CLS token plays a key role here. When ViT is trained with Global Average Pooling (GAP) instead of a CLS token, spatial localization in the patch tokens is *significantly reduced*. The CLS token acts as a dedicated "information sink" for classification, freeing the spatial tokens from having to become globally informative. This finding matters for VLMs (which we will discuss in @sec-vlm-zoo), because many VLM architectures use the *patch-level* features from the vision encoder. Those features are most spatially informative when the ViT was trained with a CLS token.

### Finding 5: Positional Embeddings Learn 2D Structure {#sec-emergent-2d}

Despite using 1D learned positional embeddings (just a lookup table with 197 entries), ViTs learn a positional encoding that reflects 2D spatial structure. If you compute the cosine similarity between the positional embedding of one patch and all other patches, the resulting similarity matrix shows clear grid patterns: patches in the same row have similar embeddings, as do patches in the same column.

![Positional embedding similarity for ViT-L/16. Each sub-plot shows the similarity between one patch's positional embedding and all others. Clear row and column structure emerges despite using 1D learned embeddings. Source: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), Appendix.](Vision Transformers and VLMs/images/vit-position-embedding-similarity.png){#fig-positional-similarity}

This emergent 2D structure is learned purely from data. The model discovers that visual patches are arranged in a 2D grid and encodes this in the positional embeddings. It is a beautiful example of how Transformers can recover spatial structure without it being architecturally imposed.

### Visualizing What Attention Heads See {#sec-attention-visualization}

One of the most compelling aspects of ViTs is the ability to visualize attention patterns. The following images from the ViT paper show attention from specific heads at different layers. Some heads clearly specialize. One might attend to horizontal edges, another to the object boundary, a third to background texture.

![Example attention maps for different heads and layers in ViT. Different heads specialize in different visual patterns — some attend to edges, others to object boundaries, others to texture. Source: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), Appendix.](Vision Transformers and VLMs/images/vit-attention-examples.png){#fig-attention-examples}

![Attention from the CLS token to all patch tokens, across different heads and layers. The CLS token gradually focuses its attention on the most informative regions of the image. Source: Dosovitskiy et al. (2020), Appendix.](Vision Transformers and VLMs/images/vit-cls-attention-heads.png){#fig-cls-attention}

But here we must issue an important warning.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: Attention weights tell you what the model considers important"}
This is one of the most pervasive misunderstandings in the ViT literature. Papers routinely plot attention maps and claim "the model attends to the dog" as evidence that the model is using the dog for its prediction. But attention weights show *where information flows*, not *what information matters*. A head might assign high attention to background patches while contributing nothing useful to the output, because the projection matrix $\mathbf{U}_{msa}$ downweights that head or because the skip connection overwhelms the attention layer's output. To truly understand what drives a ViT's prediction, you need gradient-based attribution methods (GradCAM, integrated gradients) that trace which features actually influence the loss. The attention map is a necessary but not sufficient piece of the explanation.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Think Hard: Can we just look at attention maps to understand what ViTs attend to?"}
**No.** Attention maps show where each head *directs* its attention, but this is not the same as what *contributes* to the final output. An attention head might attend broadly to the entire image (high attention everywhere) while contributing very little to the residual stream. Its output gets downweighted by the projection matrix $\mathbf{U}_{msa}$ or overwhelmed by the skip connection.

**Attention rollout** (multiplying attention matrices across layers) is a popular visualization method but fundamentally flawed. It treats all heads as equally important, ignores the skip connections, and assumes attention weights directly map to feature contributions. **Gradient-weighted attention rollout** partially addresses this by weighting each head by its gradient magnitude, but even this is an approximation.

The correct mental model: attention maps show *potential* information flow, not actual feature contribution. To understand what actually matters for the prediction, you need gradient-based methods (like GradCAM adapted for ViTs) that account for how information is used downstream.
:::

### The DINO Surprise: Self-Supervised ViTs Learn Semantic Segmentation {#sec-dino-attention}

When ViTs are trained with the DINO self-supervised method (which we will cover in detail in @sec-training-vits), their attention maps exhibit a striking property: **the self-attention of the CLS token in the final layer produces what looks like a semantic segmentation mask**, clearly delineating object boundaries, without ever seeing a single segmentation label.

This property is *specific to self-supervised ViTs*. Supervised ViTs trained on ImageNet classification do not show such clean segmentation in their attention maps. The self-supervised training objective (matching representations across different crops of the same image) appears to force the model to learn where objects are and where they end, because that information is invariant across crops and therefore useful for the self-distillation objective.

This discovery had major practical implications. It meant that DINO features could be used directly for segmentation-related tasks without any segmentation-specific training, and it suggested that self-supervised ViTs learn a more complete and structured representation of visual scenes than supervised models.

::: {.callout-tip title="Self-explanation prompt"}
If ViTs can attend globally from layer 1, why don't they just ignore local structure entirely? Think about what would happen if every head in every layer attended uniformly across the image. What useful information would be lost?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Self-explanation prompt"}
Why would a self-supervised ViT (DINO) learn better semantic segmentation maps than a supervised ViT? Think about the training objectives: classification wants to know *what* is in the image, while self-distillation across crops wants to know *what is consistent* across different views.
:::


::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: Deeper ViTs are always better"}
While scaling ViTs deeper generally improves performance, there are diminishing returns and even potential degradation. Untrained LayerNorm layers in very deep ViTs can distort representations, and the ViT-22B paper showed that training stability requires specific techniques (QK-normalization, parallel attention+FFN) at extreme depths. The "Getting ViT in Shape" (SoViT) work showed that **width should scale faster than depth**: shape-optimized ViTs with wider, shallower architectures can match models 2$\times$ their size. If you are choosing between a deeper and a wider ViT with the same parameter count, the wider one is usually the better bet.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common Misconception: ViTs can handle any visual reasoning task"}
Despite their impressive capabilities, ViTs struggle with certain types of visual reasoning that seem simple to humans: relational reasoning ("is A above B?"), counting ("how many objects?"), and compositional reasoning ("a red circle next to a blue square"). These failures persist even in very large ViTs and likely stem from the lack of explicit relational or compositional inductive biases in the self-attention mechanism. Global self-attention can *in principle* learn these relationships, but in practice the training signal from standard objectives (classification, contrastive learning, masked reconstruction) does not provide sufficient pressure to learn them. If your application requires robust spatial or compositional reasoning, be prepared for ViTs to underperform. This remains an open research challenge.
:::

---

We have now peered inside trained Vision Transformers and discovered that they build representations fundamentally different from CNNs: more uniform layers, earlier access to global information, stronger reliance on skip connections, and better preservation of spatial information. But all of this assumes you have a well-trained ViT in the first place. As we discussed in @sec-inductive-bias, training a ViT from scratch requires far more data than training a CNN. How do you train a high-quality ViT when you don't have hundreds of millions of labeled images? That is the subject of @sec-training-vits.
